rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate the six-compound elution window and identify critical pairs while minimizing the risk of missing strongly retained compounds.
The first method already achieves the maximum CRF of 1.000. Shorten the gradient by one grid step to test whether full resolution can be preserved with an earlier last peak.

Keep the fully resolving gradient and raise temperature one step to test whether retention can be shortened without losing the critical pair's resolution. Both previous methods already achieve the maximum CRF.

Shorten the gradient one step to probe the speed limit at 45 C. The critical pair is slope-sensitive, so this tests whether its improved selectivity at higher temperature provides enough resolution margin.

Narrow the solvent window to restore a slope close to the fully resolving 8-minute method while skipping its weak-solvent lead-in. The observed elution window suggests all six compounds should remain inside this gradient.

Raise temperature one step to improve the marginal critical pair and shorten retention. Earlier temperature testing improved this pair's resolution, while the other pairs currently have substantial margin.

Raise the starting organic fraction one step to shorten retention, while the resulting shallower gradient may protect the critical middle pair. Check that the first pair retains adequate resolution as early retention decreases.

Move the starting fraction up another step to reduce retention, and lower the endpoint to make the gradient shallower and support the marginal middle pair. This tests whether further window trimming preserves full resolution without compressing the early pair excessively.

Use a slightly shallower slope than injection 8 to recover the marginal middle pair, while trimming the unused high-organic tail to a four-minute gradient. The last peak previously exited near 0.49 organic, so a 0.60 endpoint should retain adequate elution strength.

With maximum-CRF methods secured, test a much steeper gradient for a faster resolving regime beyond a possible middle-pair elution-order reversal. This exploratory run will also reveal whether late-pair compression limits that approach.

Test a higher starting organic fraction with lower temperature to preserve early-pair retention and separation. This probes a different selectivity window for a shorter fully resolved method, while retaining the maximum-CRF methods already established.
Raise temperature one step from injection 9 to test a shorter fully resolved separation. The middle pair may improve, but the early pair's resolution of 1.79 makes it the likely temperature limit.

Test whether lower temperature separates the critical middle pair in the steep-gradient regime explored in injection 10. This isolates temperature selectivity while keeping the established maximum-CRF methods as fallbacks.

Refine around injection 7 with a slightly steeper gradient and a trimmed endpoint, targeting an earlier last peak. This tests whether the middle pair's small resolution margin survives the next available slope increment.

Revisit the higher starting fraction with a shallower gradient and warmer temperature than injection 11 to improve the middle pair. The lower temperature relative to injection 9 should help preserve early-pair separation despite the stronger starting solvent.

Back off the endpoint one step from injection 14 to recover full middle-pair resolution. This should provide more resolution margin than the fastest successful methods while keeping the last peak well below ten minutes.

Test a shallower gradient at 45 C to gain middle-pair resolution while preserving stronger early-pair separation than at 50 C. This targets a maximum-CRF method with greater resolution margin and a shorter separation than injection 1.

Lower temperature one step from injection 16 to strengthen early-pair separation while testing whether the middle pair remains fully resolved. This targets a compact maximum-CRF method with useful resolution margin at both critical pairs.

Lower the endpoint one step from injection 8 to recover middle-pair resolution while retaining adequate early-pair separation. This refines the fastest successful solvent window; the maximum achievable CRF is already secured.

Raise temperature one step from injection 14 to try to recover middle-pair resolution and shorten retention. The first pair may become limiting, but the lower starting fraction should preserve more early separation than in injection 12.

With the maximum CRF already secured, lower the endpoint one step from injection 16 to increase the critical middle pair's resolution margin. The last peak should still elute comfortably below ten minutes, preserving the maximum score.

Raise the starting fraction one step from injection 21 to shorten retention while retaining a shallow gradient for the middle pair. Prior runs at this starting fraction and temperature suggest the early pair should remain fully resolved.

Lower temperature one step from injection 22 to improve the limiting early pair while using the middle pair's resolution margin. This tests a nearby fully resolved alternative; the maximum CRF of 1.000 is already secured.

Raise the endpoint one step from injection 23 to shorten the separation while testing its middle-pair resolution margin. This also checks whether the fastest successful solvent program, injection 9, remains fully resolving at a temperature one step lower.

Test the remaining temperature neighbor of injection 21, whose resolution margin should accommodate modest selectivity changes while preserving maximum CRF. Injection 9 remains the fastest demonstrated fully resolved method, with its last peak at 3.40 minutes.
